power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Food insecurity is increasingly recognised as an important social determinant of eating disorder (ED) pathology.
Although research in this area has grown substantially, evidence remains fragmented across ED pathology, diagnoses, age groups, and clinical and non-clinical populations.
This review aims to update and synthesise the literature on the relationship between food insecurity and eating disorder pathology.
Relevant studies were identified by searching PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Scopus, and the grey literature up to September 2026.
Random-effects meta-analyses and narrative synthesis were carried out.
The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
Public and patient involvement and engagement informed the process throughout.
The protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261291381).
We included 140 articles in the review (n=628,090 participants) and, of these, 72 in the meta-analysis.
Food insecurity was associated with greater overall eating pathology, with pooled eORs ranging from 1.75 (1.18-2.58) to 2.36 (0.15-0.31) across the three effect-size measures.
Positive associations were also observed for binge eating, dietary restriction, purging, vomiting, and laxative use, although effect sizes varied across outcomes and analyses.
Findings were mixed for excessive exercise and negative body image, with some studies reporting significant associations with food insecurity and others finding no evidence of an association.
Overall, the included studies were of moderate to high methodological quality.

To date, the existing literature supports the role of food insecurity in the aetiology of eating disorder pathology and highlights the need for future theoretical frameworks and prevention interventions.
Food insecurity is defined as limited or uncertain access to sufficient, safe, and nutritionally adequate food (USDA Economic Research Service, 2022a).

It is a major global public health concern, affecting approximately 2.3 billion people worldwide in 2024 (28% of the global population) (UNICEF, 2025) and is associated with adverse physical and mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, stress, and suicidal ideation (see Moosavian et al., 2025, for a review).

text.text: More recently, food insecurity has been identified as a potential risk factor for eating disorder (ED) pathology (Hazzard et al., 2020), which encompasses disturbances in eating behaviours and weight-and shape-related cognitions, including dietary restraint, eating, shape and weight concerns, binge eating, avoidant or restrictive eating, and compensatory behaviours (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Fairburn & Beglin, 2008).

text.text: Given the subsequent growth of this literature, an updated synthesis is needed to clarify the breadth of associations between food insecurity and different forms of ED pathology.
Several mechanisms may explain the association between food insecurity and ED pathology.

Firstly, food insecurity may disrupt regular eating patterns through a "feast-famine" cycle, whereby periods of restricted intake during times of scarcity are followed by increased consumption when food becomes available (Dinour et al., 2007; Hamrick & Andrews, 2016; Hazzard et al., 2023).

text.text: Indeed, meta-analytic evidence shows that food-insecure adults have 66% higher odds of binge eating and 2.7-fold higher odds of binge-eating disorder than food-secure adults (Abene et al., 2024).

text.text: The "famine" component of food insecurity may likewise also be relevant to restrictive eating pathology.

Although restriction remains comparatively understudied, emerging evidence suggests that limiting intake during food insecurity may serve both resource-conservation and weight-control functions, with these motivations often cooccurring (Karvay et al., 2025).

text.text: However, the extent to which food insecurity is associated with restrictive ED pathology has yet to be systematically quantified.
Another potential mechanism linking food insecurity to ED pathology may operate through body image.

Food insecurity may increase reliance on inexpensive, energy-dense foods and limit access to structured physical activity, potentially contributing to higher body weight and widening the discrepancy between an individual's perceived body and culturally valued appearance ideals (Domingo et al., 2021; Lamont & Speed, 2025).

Recently, some research has even suggested that food insecurity may also contribute to avoidant or restrictive eating in young people (Berge et al., 2020).

text.text: Accordingly, the present systematic review and meta-analysis aim to (a) provide an updated synthesis of associations between food insecurity and ED pathology across symptom domains, diagnoses, and diverse populations, and (b) quantify the strength and consistency of these associations through meta-analysis.
This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Page et al., 2021).

text.text: The protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261291381).
A systematic and comprehensive search was conducted across nine electronic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, ProQuest, ET, medRxiv, and PsyArXiv.
The final search was conducted in September 2026.
No restrictions were applied by publication date or language during the search.

The final search combined food insecurity terms with ED pathology terms including ED diagnoses, binge eating, restrictive eating, dieting, fasting, purging, compensatory behaviours, ARFID, PICA, excessive exercise, body dissatisfaction, and body image concerns.
The full reported search strategies for each database is located in Table S2.

text.text: Eligible studies included participants of all age groups from either clinical or general population samples.
Studies were required to include measures of both food insecurity and eating pathology (e.g., body image concerns or disordered eating).

Quantitative studies examining the association between FI and ED outcomes were included, including crosssectional and longitudinal observational studies, as well as randomized and non-randomized studies as well as randomised and non-randomised intervention studies that reported associations between the two constructs.
For intervention studies, associations based on baseline measures (pre-intervention) were extracted where available.
Studies were excluded if they involved non-human subjects, did not assess both food insecurity and ED pathology, or used qualitative designs.
Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses were also excluded.

Articles identified through the literature search were uploaded to Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016), where duplicates were identified using the automated duplicate-detection function and manually checked where necessary.

text.text: Following deduplication, two reviewers (AMN and GP) independently screened titles and abstracts against the review's eligibility criteria.
Both reviewers initially screened 10% of records independently to assess inter-rater agreement.
Following two rounds of calibration, Cohen's kappa exceeded 0.80, after which the remaining records were screened independently by both reviewers.
Full-text screening was conducted by four reviewers (FT, GP, AN, and CW) working in pairs, with each paper assessed independently by two reviewers.
Each pair initially screened 10% of reports to establish inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ > 0.80), before independently screening the remaining reports.

text.text: Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus among the reviewers.
A data extraction form was developed and piloted on 10% of included studies.
Two reviewer pairs (GP and FT; AMN and CW) independently extracted data, achieving over 90% agreement during piloting.
text.formatted: Two reviewer pairs <ref type="bibr">(GP and FT; AMN and CW)</ref> independently extracted data, achieving over 90% agreement during piloting.

text.text: The remaining studies were extracted independently, with discrepancies resolved through discussion.

The following information was extracted from each included study: author, year of publication, sample size, country, mean age and standard deviation, socioeconomic status, race and ethnicity, sex assigned at birth and gender (n, %), body mass index (mean, SD), sample characteristics (e.g., community or clinical sample), study design, measure of food insecurity, measure of ED pathology, effect size type, overall findings, and covariates included in adjusted analyses.
Where information was unclear or not reported in the published article, study authors were contacted for additional data/clarification.
Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT; 2018), comprising two screening questions and five design-specific criteria across different study designs.
Although the review's eligibility criteria permitted a range of methodologies, only quantitative findings contributed to the final synthesis and meta-analysis.
Studies were therefore appraised using the quantitative descriptive criteria for non-comparative studies (MMAT; Hong et al., 2018).

text.text: The criteria assess methodological rigour, including the appropriateness of the sampling strategy, representativeness of the sample, quality of outcome measurement, risk of non-response bias, and appropriateness of the statistical analyses.
Where an included report used a mixed-methods design, only its quantitative component was appraised because only quantitative findings were extracted and synthesized.
The same procedure for assessing inter-rater agreement was used for quality assessment.
Two reviewer pairs (GP and FT; AMN and CW) independently assessed the included studies (after 90% agreement was reached), with discrepancies resolved through discussion.

text.text: A lived-experience advisory group comprising two individuals with experience of both food insecurity and EDs and one individual with experience of food insecurity and caring for a child with an ED, contributed to the development of the review protocol.
Through group discussions, contributors affirmed the relevance of the research questions and emphasised the importance of examining food insecurity across a broad spectrum of ED pathology.
They encouraged the inclusion of less frequently studied ED presentations, particularly ARFID, which informed the review's broad scope and search strategy.

Contributors also influenced the eligibility criteria, highlighting the relevance of food insecurity and ED pathology during childhood and adolescence, informing the decision to include populations of all ages.

Contributors further highlighted how food insecurity and ED pathology can coexist with other physical and mental health conditions, informing the decision not to exclude studies involving individuals with comorbidities.

Contributors also co interpreted the findings and offered possible explanations for the mixed results concerning excessive exercise, body image, and ARFID-related pathology, informing their interpretation in the discussion.

As studies reported associations between food insecurity and eating pathology using different effect-size metrics (e.g., odds ratios (ORs), prevalence ratio (PR); raw frequency of food insecurity and ED outcome, and correlation coefficients), we conducted separate metaanalysis for each effect size metrics to pool to effect sizes.

To facilitate comparison across the different types of pooled effect estimates reported across meta-analyses, we followed the approach recommended by Fusar-Poli and Radua (2018) and converted all pooled effect estimates into equivalent odds ratios (eORs), using the effectsize package in R (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020).

Effect sizes were extracted for all relevant outcomes and grouped into domains (e.g., body dissatisfaction, shape concerns, and muscularity concerns were grouped under body image).
To ensure effect-size independence (Cheung, 2019), each meta-analysis included only one effect size per unique sample.

text.text: Where multiple eligible outcomes were reported, the outcome most frequently assessed across studies was selected.
All analyses were conducted in R (version 3.6.0) using the metafor package.
Due to the included studies having a variety of measurements, ages, and sample characteristics, a random effects model was selected.

Heterogeneity across studies was assessed with the I² statistic and Cochran's Q test (Higgins et al., 2003), with I² values around 25%, 50%, and above 75% taken to indicate low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al., 2003).

text.text: Four longitudinal studies had data available for the meta-analysis.

Given this small number, estimates from both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies were pooled, and the influence of longitudinal estimates on the results was assessed using the aforementioned sensitivity analyses.
Because the number of included studies was small; moderator analyses were limited to three variables: (1) age (2) gender (quantified as % of women in each sample) (3) publication year.
Moderator analyses were carried out on variables which were reported in a minimum of six studies (Fu et al, 2011).

text.text: This included studies that reported only the direction or significance of an association without sufficient data to calculate an effect size, and studies whose estimates could not be meaningfully pooled due to differences in how food insecurity or eating pathology was measured or categorised.
Studies reporting adjusted effect estimates were also synthesised narratively when differences in the covariates included in their models made the estimates unsuitable for pooling.

text.text: The literature search identified 3,101 records, of which 1,277 duplicates were removed, leaving 1,824 records for title and abstract screening.
Following screening, 1,463 records were excluded, and 361 reports underwent full-text eligibility assessment.
Of these, 221 were excluded, resulting in 140 articles being included in the systematic review.
Of the included articles, 72 contributed to the meta-analyses, while the remaining 68 were synthesised narratively due to unavailable effect estimates for quantitative pooling.

Authors of 63 potentially eligible studies were contacted for clarification or additional data; 27 responded, and five provided data enabling inclusion (Arikawa et al., 2020; Hazzard et al., 2023b; Julceus et al., 2025; Rancourt et al., 2023; Rodrigues et al., 2026).

text.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis provided evidence of consistent associations between food insecurity and a broad spectrum of ED pathology, including overall ED psychopathology, binge eating, dietary restriction, and compensatory behaviours such as purging, self-induced vomiting and laxative use.
However, findings for excessive exercise, body image concerns and ED diagnoses were more mixed.
The follow-up meta-regression analysis suggested that the associations were mostly consistent across gender and age.

Our meta-analyses identified associations between food insecurity and both binge eating and restriction, with a more extensive evidence base for binge eating across adults and young people, extending previous findings (Abene et al., 2023).

text.text: Our findings support the feast-famine hypothesis, whereby restriction and binge eating may reflect different phases of disrupted food access.

However, prospective evidence remains limited and mixed, and some binge-eating associations attenuated after sociodemographic adjustment (Goode et al., 2021) or accounting for financial and psychological factors (Simone et al., 2021).

text.text: One possible explanation is provided by the stress-process model, which proposes that social circumstances influence psychological distress through chronic strains and access to coping resources (Pearlin et al., 1981).

text.text: Indeed, binge eating may represent an attempt to manage distress, raising the possibility that psychological factors are not simply confounders but part of the pathway linking food insecurity to binge eating (Haedt-Matt & Keel, 2011).

text.text: Longitudinal research is needed to clarify temporal relationships and distinguish confounding from mediation.
Food insecurity was associated with purging behaviours, including self-induced vomiting and laxative use.

Feast-famine cycles may involve restriction during food scarcity followed by perceived overeating when food becomes available, potentially triggering weight-gain concerns and compensatory purging, consistent with the cognitive behavioural model of bulimia nervosa (Fairburn et al., 2003).

text.text: In contrast, findings for excessive exercise were mixed, potentially reflecting the lack of a clear theoretical pathway linking it to food insecurity.

For example, Chaimano et al. (2026) found an indirect association between food insecurity and exercise addiction through muscle dysmorphia, suggesting that body-image concerns may contribute to the relationship between food insecurity and pathological or compensatory exercise.

(2026)</ref> found an indirect association between food insecurity and exercise addiction through muscle dysmorphia, suggesting that body-image concerns may contribute to the relationship between food insecurity and pathological or compensatory exercise.

text.text: Findings were also mixed regarding body image concerns which may reflect differences in the constructs assessed, including body dissatisfaction, thinness concerns, muscularity and appearance evaluation.

Many measures emphasised thin-ideal pressures, despite body-size preferences varying across cultural and socioeconomic contexts (Ogden & Thomas, 1999; Wardle & Griffith, 2001), potentially overlooking preferences of food-insecure individuals.

text.text: Indeed, Lauten et al. (2026) found that whilst food-insecure adults reported greater body dissatisfaction, they were also more likely to prefer a larger body or maintain their current size.

text.text: Thus, body dissatisfaction among food-insecure individuals may not reflect a desire for thinness, highlighting the limitations of measures focused on thinness concerns.
Across the meta-analyses, food insecurity was consistently linked to greater overall ED psychopathology, in line with Hazzard et al. (2020).

text.text: In contrast, the pooled association with ED diagnosis was positive but non-significant.

This may partly reflect limited statistical power due to the small number of studies, alongside socioeconomic inequalities in ED recognition and access to care, as individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds are less likely to receive a diagnosis or specialist treatment despite experiencing symptoms (Sonneville & Lipson, 2018).

text.text: Evidence for ARFID-related symptoms and diabetes-specific disordered eating was likewise mixed and based on few studies, therefore firm conclusions cannot be drawn and further research is needed.
A key limitation is the geographical concentration of the evidence, with 105 studies conducted in the US.
This may limit the generalisability of the findings as the experience of food insecurity is partly shaped by country-specific welfare and food-assistance systems.
In the US, SNAP benefits are typically distributed monthly, which may contribute to fluctuations in food availability across the benefit cycle (Hazzard et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the US, SNAP benefits are typically distributed monthly, which may contribute to fluctuations in food availability across the benefit cycle <ref type="bibr">(Hazzard et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These mechanisms may vary across welfare systems and payment schedules, with cross-national evidence showing differences in the strength of associations between food insecurity and ED behaviours (Efstate et al., 2025).

text.text: Future research outside the US is therefore needed to establish generalisability of the findings globally.
Two field-specific methodological limitations warrant consideration.

First, the small number of studies contributing to several meta-analyses limited our ability to explore sources of heterogeneity (e.g., individual-versus household-level food insecurity), although moderator analyses did not indicate that age or gender significantly influenced effect estimates.
Second, the few longitudinal studies, many of which drew on overlapping cohorts and examined different ED outcomes, further precluded meaningful comparisons of effect estimates across study designs.
Additionally, studies contributing to adjusted odds-ratio meta-analyses controlled for different demographic, socioeconomic and psychological factors, reducing comparability of pooled estimates.
This is particularly important given evidence that food insecurity is associated with ED pathology beyond broader socioeconomic disadvantage (Hazzard et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This is particularly important given evidence that food insecurity is associated with ED pathology beyond broader socioeconomic disadvantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Hazzard et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Inappropriate adjustment may introduce bias, as variables such as weight status may act as confounders (e.g., through weight-related discrimination and financial disadvantage), mediators, or colliders depending on the causal relationship between food insecurity and ED pathology (Hazzard et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Inappropriate adjustment may introduce bias, as variables such as weight status may act as confounders (e.g., through weight-related discrimination and financial disadvantage), mediators, or colliders depending on the causal relationship between food insecurity and ED pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Hazzard et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should therefore pre-specify causal assumptions and use theory-informed confounder selection.

Future research should also move beyond documenting associations to focus on two key priorities: first, establishing causal relationships between food insecurity and ED pathology; and second, investigating how food insecurity can be identified and addressed within ED care.

Indeed, growing evidence suggests that food insecurity can interfere with treatment by worsening mental health (Bek et al., 2023) and limiting access to food and making recommendations such as regular eating and structured meal plans difficult to follow (Bryson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Indeed, growing evidence suggests that food insecurity can interfere with treatment by worsening mental health <ref type="bibr">(Bek et al., 2023)</ref> and limiting access to food and making recommendations such as regular eating and structured meal plans difficult to follow <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Bryson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: ED clinicians have also reported limited knowledge and guidance for managing food insecurity, highlighting the need for routine screening, formal training, financially realistic treatment planning, and clear referral pathways to food or financial support (Kuehne et al., 2023).
text.formatted: ED clinicians have also reported limited knowledge and guidance for managing food insecurity, highlighting the need for routine screening, formal training, financially realistic treatment planning, and clear referral pathways to food or financial support <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Kuehne et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Policy implications also warrant investigation as changes could exacerbate food insecurity.

For example, in the US, withdrawal of enhanced SNAP benefits in 2023 was associated with increased food insecurity (Richterman et al., 2023) and poorer physical, but not mental, health outcomes (Liu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, in the US, withdrawal of enhanced SNAP benefits in 2023 was associated with increased food insecurity <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Richterman et al., 2023)</ref> and poorer physical, but not mental, health outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Liu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, ED outcomes were not assessed, leaving it unclear whether such policy changes also influence ED risk, symptom severity, or recovery.

Natural-experiment studies examining ED outcomes before and after changes to food-assistance policies could help identify potential unintended consequences and inform policies that protect both food security and ED-related health outcomes.

Overall, this review provides consistent evidence of associations between food insecurity and a broad spectrum of ED pathology, highlighting its potential importance in the development and maintenance of ED symptoms and its relevance to clinical practice.
